text_blocks.snippet: Treatment for high blood pressure (hypertension) combines heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when needed, prescription medications.
snippet_highlighted_words: heart-healthy lifestyle changes and, when needed, prescription medications

text_blocks.snippet: Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone with elevated blood pressure or hypertension, and can sometimes reduce or delay the need for medication:

list.snippet: DASH Eating Plan: Follow a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products, while cutting back on saturated fat and cholesterol (such as the NHLBI DASH Eating Plan).
Reduce Sodium: Lower daily salt and sodium intake (aiming for less than 2,000 mg or lower per day).
Regular Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (like brisk walking, cycling, or swimming).
Weight Management: Lose extra weight if overweight or obese to ease the workload on your heart.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Avoid heavy alcohol use and stop smoking cigarettes or using tobacco, which immediately narrows blood vessels.
Improve Sleep: Aim for at least 7 hours of quality sleep per night.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately upon diagnosis if your blood pressure is very high or you have high cardiovascular risk, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—your doctor may prescribe medication. Common first-line classes include:

list.snippet: ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme inhibitors): e.g., lisinopril, ramipril; they keep blood vessels from narrowing.
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): e.g., losartan, valsartan; they block the effects of chemicals that narrow blood vessels.
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem; they relax and widen blood vessels by preventing calcium from entering muscle cells.
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): e.g., thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide or chlorthalidone; they help the body flush out excess sodium and water.

text_blocks.snippet: If blood pressure remains uncontrolled (resistant hypertension) or if you have specific heart or kidney conditions, your doctor may add other classes:

list.snippet: Beta-Blockers: e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol; often used if you have a history of heart attack, heart failure, or fast heart rate.
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists / Spironolactone: Blocks aldosterone to help remove extra fluid.
Central-Acting Agents or Vasodilators: e.g., clonidine or hydralazine, used in specific multi-drug regimens.

text_blocks.snippet: Many people require a combination of two or more blood pressure drugs—often available in a single daily pill—to reach their target blood pressure (typically less than 130/80 mm Hg for most adults). You can explore detailed medication guides through the American Heart Association Blood Pressure Medications.
